title: flagd Reference
bottom_line: When you work with flagd feature flags, Claude uses this reference to write flag files, run flagd, connect your app and fix failures without browsing.

sections.heading: Type the command or just talk about flagd

blocks.caption: The command takes no arguments. You can also skip it: the skill starts on its own.

blocks.title: Two ways the skill starts

nodes.label: You mention flagd or its parts

blocks.caption: You do not need to say "flagd". flagd is the reference OpenFeature backend, so related requests start the skill too.

blocks.text: **flagd** (https://flagd.dev) is the CNCF/OpenFeature feature-flag evaluation engine. A **feature flag** is a switch that turns a feature on or off, or picks one of several variants. flagd has no UI and no database: the flag file is the source of truth, kept in git.

`fractional` or `sem_ver` targeting
the OpenFeature flagd provider in any language (Go, Java, Node, web, Python, .NET, PHP, Rust)

sections.heading: Ask for a 10% rollout and get a ready flag

before.label: You ask
before.text: "Add a 10% rollout of `new-checkout` to our flagd config."

after.label: Claude delivers
after.text: A flag whose targeting uses `fractional`, which buckets users by their `targetingKey`, plus a reminder that your application must pass a `targetingKey`.

blocks.caption: The example from the plugin's README.

blocks.title: The reminder that comes with it
blocks.text: Your application must pass a `targetingKey` (for example the user id) in the evaluation context. Without one, the evaluation fails and your code falls back to its default value.

sections.heading: Claude follows seven rules that prevent common flag mistakes

cards.title: Always set targetingKey
cards.text: Needed for `fractional` rollouts with the default bucketing.

cards.title: Return variant names
cards.text: Targeting returns a variant name, never a value.

cards.title: Validate before deploying
cards.text: Use `.flagd.json` naming and `$schema`, and validate in CI.

cards.title: No UI by design
cards.text: Flags live in files you control.

cards.title: Say which source it used
cards.text: When the bundled docs are silent.

blocks.caption: Each rule in full is in the list below.

blocks.title: The rules in full
items: Always set `targetingKey` in evaluation context when a flag uses `fractional` with the default bucketing; without it the evaluation errors and falls to the code default. To bucket on another attribute, pass an expression (e.g. `{"var":"email"}`) as the first `fractional` element.
Targeting must return a variant name, not a value. `"if":[cond, true]` is a bug; write `"if":[cond, "on"]`.
Keep all variants the same type and call the matching `get<Type>Value`; a type mismatch gives a `TYPE_MISMATCH` error and the code default.
Prefer `.flagd.json` naming plus `$schema` so editors validate, and validate in CI before deploying. A malformed file is rejected as a whole and flagd keeps serving the previous good state.

Don't reach for a UI: flagd has none by design. Flags live in git, a ConfigMap or an HTTP endpoint you control. If you want a hosted UI, Claude points you at OpenFeature-compatible vendors, but flagd itself stays file-driven.
Check `reason` and `errorCode` before blaming targeting: `DEFAULT` means the rule evaluated but matched nothing; `FLAG_NOT_FOUND` often means the wrong selector or flag set.

When the bundled docs are silent or ambiguous, Claude reads the live page on https://flagd.dev/, greps the source (`git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/open-feature/flagd`), or searches issues on https://github.com/open-feature/flagd/issues, and says which source it used.

sections.heading: The skill needs nothing; running its output needs flagd and an SDK

cards.title: The skill itself
cards.text: No requirements, no arguments and no environment variables.

cards.title: Running what it writes
cards.text: flagd (as a Docker image, a binary or on Kubernetes) and, in your application, the OpenFeature SDK with the flagd provider for your language.

blocks.title: Environment variables
blocks.text: None are required by the skill itself. flagd and its providers read `FLAGD_*` variables; these are documented in the skill's reference files.
